catalyst.body:

Creativity requires a catalyst. It is a reaction to something you notice.

catalyst-collision-exposure.body:
The more reactions you will have. 

You cannot control how or when all of the information combines, and sparks creativity, but you can understand why it happens and give yourself more opportunities to experience it.

catalyst-outcomes-exposure.body:
Exposure is not a direct catalyst like the two categories we have already covered. 

It isn't the result of interacting with the product or project you are working on.

It's alll of the things that influence the way you solve problems and think that come from everywhere else beside the product or project you are working on.

When you see novel solutions. Solutions that make you stop and say…how did they even come up with that. 

That is because of this.

Exposure is creative fuel. It gives you new patterns and possibilities.

What do I mean?

catalyst-outcomes-feedback.body:
So, feedback gives us evidence. It tells us explicitly "here is what happened"

Next let's talk about friction. Friction is when reality does not match expectation. Friction says “Something is off” it is different from feedback, because friction requires you to be hands on. It isn't something tangible it is something we feel while in the act of doing.

catalyst-outcomes-friction.body:
Feedback tells you what happened.

Friction tells you when something feels off. 

Exposure gives you possibility.

catalyst-reprise.body:
Catalysts from the work give you direction. They tell you where to pay attention.

But knowing where to focus does not tell you what to create.

For that you need another kind of catalyst. Can you guess why this one is named "from the world?"

When you see novel solutions. Solutions that make you stop and say…how did they even come up with that.

That is because of these right here.

These represent allll of the things you have seen, learned, and experienced outside of the work you do that shape the way you solve problems.

They are responsible for expanding the range of connections you are capable of making.

What do I mean?

friction.body:
There are so many different reasons for friction.

Some are easy to spot.

It's really obvious when you notice that the same state exists across 5 different locations when it should live in only 1.

Some are...not, and they are the hidden cases of misalignment that make you pull your hair out trying to figure out why something isn't working or why users are behaving a certain way.

So how can you get better at finding friction?

friction-practice-aperture.body: Zoom out on what you're working on.

friction-practice-aperture-expanded.body: and take a look at the bigger picture.

friction-practice-aperture-focus.body: Zoom in. Dive into the details and pull apart why each piece is needed?

friction-practice-aperture-network.body:
Take a look at what happened before. What happens after?

The more information you consume, the more context you have, the higher the ceiling will be on your creativity.

friction-practice-aperture-prompt.body:

friction-practice-ask-why.body: When the cost of writing, and refactoring code is 0 what is the incentive to write smaller functions? Does it still exist? Maybe it does in some cases maybe it goes away entirely?

friction-practice-prompt.body: The best thing you can do is pause and ask why. You may recognize these knuckleheads. The conversation they are having is perfect example of this.

friction-practice-unspoken.body:
Finally, pay attention to what people do not say.

There is a fundamental truth to human psychology.

The moment experience becomes explanation, it starts to drift. Not because people are lying, but because they are translating. They are trying, usually with good intention, to share the parts they think are important, in a way they think will be helpful for you.

Often times this results in the real source of friction being filtered out of the story

So the best thing you can do is experience reality as it is.

less-sacred-constraints.body:
Sometimes it isn't getting started that is tough. It is getting past a dead end. Artificial Contraints are exactly what they sound like.

"What if I could only use one color", "What if I we only used a single API endpoint?"

Forced connections is the same goal but instead of limiting what is possible, you are forcing together two unrelated ideas and seeing what shakes out.

"What if API responses worked like GPS directions?"

"What if search worked like a public library?"

What these exercises produce don't have to be used, but they can shake things up and get you out of a creative rut.

reality-practice-output-artifacts.body:
If there is one lesson you get about creativity from my entire talk it is this.

The output of creativity is not the artifacts you make along the way. The output is the clarity you gain making them.

Artifacts are not precious. They are not special. They are a tool. A means to an end.

Making something real gives the work a chance to answer back. It turns assumptions into evidence, exposes what you still do not understand, and gives you something new to react to.

That reaction becomes the next catalyst, carrying you through the loop again and again until the answer becomes clear.

The last thing we are going to cover today. One of the easiest traps to fall into with creative work. You get over the hurdle of the “blank canvas” and get started, but then you try to solve the whole world. All at one time.

When you try to solve everything, you end up solving nothing.

It’s overwhelming. It’s too much to solve at once. So either you give up, or you get lost.

taste-pattern-matching.body:
Taste is pattern matching earned through pain.

We have been over this. Creativity isn’t magic. Neither is “taste”.

You know, there was this story I always heard as a kid, and when I heard it I remember it blowing my mind. It was about the people who worked for the government or banks whose job it was to detect counterfeit bills and they didn't use a special machine, they didn't use one of those markers. They could just touch a bill and know. It felt off. 

They had touched soooo many bills that they could immediately tell the difference between what was real and what was fake.
